You may see headlines about “close shaves,” but those are flybys, not collisions. For example, one well-known asteroid, 1999 AN10, is expected to pass safely in 2027 at roughly Moon-like distances—close in space terms, but a miss all the same.

Here’s how we know. After discovery, astronomers track an asteroid over many nights and calculate its path. Early on, the path has a fuzzy “corridor” of possibilities—like seeing a car’s headlights far away in fog. As more measurements come in, that corridor narrows. Initial tiny “maybe” impact odds almost always shrink to zero. That’s why sensational early numbers can sound scary but usually vanish with better data.

Tiny space pebbles do hit Earth every day and burn up harmlessly; house-sized ones can make a loud fireball once in a while. City-block or larger objects—the kind that could cause serious damage—are rare, and none is on course for next year. If you want the latest, check NASA’s CNEOS Sentry Risk Table or ESA’s NEO Coordination Centre; they’re the scoreboards the professionals use.

What we usually call “steam” is the white cloud you can see, but that cloud isn’t steam at all—it’s a tiny fog of liquid water droplets. Real steam (water vapor) is invisible, just like the moisture in the air on a humid day. You only see a cloud when that invisible vapor cools down and condenses into countless tiny droplets, the way your breath turns into a little cloud on a cold morning.

While the burner is on, the air right above the pot is very hot and racing upward. In that hot, fast plume, the water vapor stays too warm to condense nearby, so the visible cloud either forms higher up, or not at all if the kitchen air is warm. When you turn off the heat, the plume slows and cools. The vapor now lingers and mixes with cooler room air sooner, so it condenses right above the pot and—poof—a white cloud appears. Think of it like a hot-air elevator versus an escalator: with the elevator (burner on), the vapor shoots past the lobby before it can turn into fog; with the slower escalator (burner off), it hangs around the lobby long enough to form the visible mist.

“Photons don’t experience time or space” is a shorthand for a precise idea: along a light path the “proper time” is zero, so there is no meaningful rest frame in which a photon carries its own clock or ruler. But physics does not need the photon’s own watch to define its properties. Observers—us, our detectors, telescopes—use their clocks and rulers to measure the light’s energy, color (frequency), direction, and polarization as that light passes by. Think of a train whistle: the whistle doesn’t need to “experience” anything for people on the platform to hear a higher pitch as it approaches and a lower pitch as it recedes. The pitch is a relation between the source, the listener, and their motion.

A photon’s “varying” properties are exactly these relations changing. If the source or observer moves, the measured frequency shifts (the Doppler effect). If light climbs out of a gravitational field or rides the expanding fabric of the universe, its wavelength stretches (gravitational and cosmological redshift). If it passes through matter or a magnetic field, its direction or polarization can rotate or scatter. None of this requires a photon’s internal clock; it’s the environment and the observer’s frame slicing up the same electromagnetic ripple in different ways. In more visual terms: imagine a diagonal wavefront crossing a grid. Different tilted grids (different states of motion or gravity) count different spacings and rates as the same ripple goes by.

Some features don’t vary: in empty space every observer agrees that light moves at the same speed and that a free photon has no rest mass. Others, like energy and wavelength, are frame-dependent and interaction-dependent. So the fact that a photon carries no wristwatch doesn’t make it property-less; it just means its measurable traits live in the relationships between source, path, and observer, not in an imagined “photon’s point of view.”

The “speed of light” is really the speed of cause and effect. It’s the fastest pace at which any influence—light, gravity, electricity, information—can ripple through space. Picture a stone dropped in a pond: the ripples spread outward and define which leaves can be reached and when. In spacetime, those ripples form a growing bubble around any event. That bubble’s edge expands at one universal rate, c. If something could outrun that edge, different observers could disagree about what happened first—messages could arrive before they were sent—breaking cause and effect. So c isn’t a posted speed limit enforced by cosmic police; it’s the way the map of space and time is drawn.

Why can’t we just push harder to reach it? As an object moves faster, each extra push buys less speed and more “distortion” of time and space: its time runs slower and distances in its direction shrink, from the viewpoint of an outside observer. The energy cost ramps up so sharply that reaching c would require infinite energy for anything with mass. Massless things, like light, have no choice but to move at c; anything with mass must stay below. A useful image is a treadmill that speeds up as you run: you can get astonishingly close to the belt’s top speed, but every extra step costs more effort and adds almost no progress.

Two common caveats: light can be slowed in glass or water, but c refers to empty space—the ultimate speed of information. And distant galaxies can seem to separate faster than c because space itself is stretching; that’s not motion through space, so it doesn’t carry messages faster than c locally. In every local race to send a signal from A to B, c is the unbeatable pace set by the geometry of the universe.

Short answer: not a surface, because a black hole has no solid surface to spin. What “rotates” is the spacetime geometry itself—the gravitational field. A rotating (Kerr) black hole carries angular momentum, and that twists the fabric of space and time around it. If you floated near it with a perfect gyroscope, the local “rest frame” you’d try to keep would be gently turned, as if space were a thick syrup being stirred. This effect is called frame dragging: nearby everything, even light, is compelled to swirl around with the hole.

You can think of three related pieces. First, the matter that collapsed had some spin; that angular momentum is conserved and becomes a property of the black hole. Second, the event horizon is not a material shell, but it does have a well-defined “angular velocity”—the pattern of light that skims along the horizon co-rotates, much like stripes painted on a whirlpool that you can only see from afar. Third, just outside the horizon lies the ergosphere, a region where space is dragged so strongly that nothing can remain “stationary” relative to distant stars; everything is carried along like leaves caught in a vortex. So while the accretion disk and jets you may see are ordinary matter in motion, the core rotation is the twist of spacetime itself, not a spinning surface.

Short answer: yes—if you squeeze water hard enough, it can freeze into a solid even at room temperature. Think of water molecules as people at a concert. When there’s space, they mill around (liquid). Pack them tightly enough and they’re forced into orderly rows (solid). For water, that orderly, high-pressure solid shows up around a billion pascals of pressure, roughly 10,000 times atmospheric pressure—far beyond anything in everyday life, but common deep inside large icy moons and exoplanets. Under those conditions water forms “high-pressure ices” (like ice VI or ice VII) that are actually denser than liquid water.

Here’s the twist: at ordinary pressures, the familiar ice in your freezer is puffier than liquid water—it floats. So, if you press on regular ice a little, you encourage it to melt rather than freeze. That counterintuitive behavior helps explain why ice can be slippery: pressure can locally melt a thin film of water. But keep turning up the pressure and new, tightly packed crystal structures become more favorable, and compression flips from melting to freezing. In practice, you’d also need to manage the heat generated by squeezing; compressing raises temperature, so experiments typically remove heat to let the solid form.

Space isn’t a material the way wood or water is. It’s more like the stage on which everything happens—the distances and directions between things. On everyday scales it seems empty, and even between stars and galaxies it’s an extreme vacuum: imagine a stadium-sized volume containing only a few lonely atoms, with occasional specks of dust and fast-moving particles. Threading through that emptiness is light of all kinds—radio, infrared, visible, X-rays—and a drizzle of ghostly neutrinos passing unnoticed.

But “empty” space is not blank. It’s filled with invisible fields—like magnetic and gravitational fields—that exist everywhere and can carry energy. According to quantum physics, even the quietest vacuum fizzes with tiny, fleeting jitters, a bit like a pond that looks calm from afar but up close is dimpled by minuscule ripples. These ever-present fields are the medium through which light travels and forces act.

On the largest scales, space itself can bend and stretch. Gravity, in Einstein’s picture, is the curvature of this cosmic fabric, and titanic events can send ripples through it as gravitational waves. Most of the universe’s content is also invisible to us: dark matter, an unseen scaffolding that guides the formation of galaxies, and dark energy, a kind of energy woven into space that makes the expansion of the universe speed up. So space isn’t made of a single “stuff”; it’s a flexible geometry sparsely sprinkled with matter and permeated by a sea of fields and energy.

I can’t tell without seeing your exact setup, but here’s the Monty Hall “shape” to compare against. Picture a game show with three doors: one hides a car, two hide goats. You pick a door. The host, who knows where the car is, always opens a different door to reveal a goat and then always offers you the chance to switch. Under these rules, switching wins 2/3 of the time because your first pick is a 1/3 long shot, and the host’s reveal funnels the remaining 2/3 chance onto the other unopened door.

Your problem is effectively the same if it follows that pattern, even if it’s dressed up differently or has more doors. It is not the same if the “host” doesn’t know where the prize is, might accidentally reveal it, chooses randomly which door to open, sometimes refuses to open a door, or decides whether to offer switching based on your initial choice. Any of those tweaks change the odds and break the Monty Hall structure.

It’s true that Lactobacillus bacteria are common in the vagina, where they act like friendly “bouncers,” keeping the environment slightly acidic and discouraging troublemakers. The gut also hosts Lactobacillus, but it’s a different neighborhood with different rules and residents. Swallowing small amounts of vaginal bacteria during oral sex hasn’t been shown to improve digestion or gut health. Most microbes encountered this way face saliva enzymes and stomach acid—like tossing a handful of garden seeds into a hot furnace—so very few would survive, and the doses are tiny compared with probiotic foods or supplements specifically designed to deliver large numbers of well-studied strains.

On the other hand, oral sex can transmit infections such as HPV, gonorrhea, syphilis, chlamydia, and herpes, including to the throat. So the potential risks are known, while digestive benefits are unproven. If your goal is a healthier microbiome, the boring but reliable options work best: fiber-rich foods, fermented foods like yogurt or kefir, and, when appropriate, probiotics with documented strains and doses. Enjoy oral sex for intimacy and pleasure if you wish, but don’t count on it as a digestion booster. If you want to reduce infection risk, barrier methods (like dental dams) help.

Short answer: most large galaxies seem to have a heavyweight in the downtown district, and it’s usually a supermassive black hole. We infer this from how stars and gas whip around the center: their speeds require an enormous amount of mass crammed into a tiny volume. In our own Milky Way, for example, we track stars orbiting an invisible object about four million times the Sun’s mass packed into a region far smaller than our solar system—behavior that matches a black hole and leaves little room for alternatives. When these central black holes actively swallow gas, the infall lights up the core as a quasar or active galactic nucleus; when they’re “on a diet,” the galaxy center looks quiet.

But “every galaxy” is too strong. Smaller and dwarf galaxies don’t always show evidence for a central black hole. Some host a different kind of central heavyweight: a very dense cluster of ordinary stars, like a crowded town square rather than a single skyscraper. A few may have both a star cluster and a modest black hole, and some may have neither an obvious black hole nor a particularly massive cluster. So while big galaxies almost always carry a central black hole, the smallest galaxies are a mixed bag.

If you do find a single, very compact mass dominating a galaxy’s very center, then yes—by the process of elimination it’s essentially necessarily a black hole. Other ideas (like a tight ball of dead stars or dark matter) either can’t be packed that densely without falling apart or would reveal themselves in other ways. So: many galaxies have a massive central something; in large galaxies that “something” is almost always a black hole, whereas in small galaxies it can be a black hole, a dense star cluster, both, or neither.

Eyes don’t see the world in “frames.” Vision is more like a flowing stream than a flipbook: light is continuous, and your brain keeps updating its picture of the world. How smooth that picture feels depends on brightness, contrast, where on the retina the image lands (center vs. edges), and whether you’re sensing flicker or tracking motion. A useful idea here is the “flicker fusion” point—the rate at which a blinking light stops looking like a blink and starts looking steady. For most everyday conditions, that point sits around 50–90 times per second.

Push the conditions, and the numbers climb. In bright light and especially in your peripheral vision, people can detect changes above 100 Hz, and brief flashes only a few milliseconds long can be noticed—so in some ways we can react to events spaced hundreds of times per second. That’s why 24 fps movies look smooth (they use motion blur to help), 60 Hz screens feel clearly smoother, and 120–144 Hz displays look crisper and can aid fast tracking and reduce eye strain, with smaller gains beyond that. So the better question is not “what FPS can the eye see,” but “how quickly can we notice changes?” Answer: roughly dozens to a couple of hundred times per second, depending on the scene and the task—like a ceiling fan that looks like a solid disk at one speed, but whose blades you can still catch at the edges when it spins even faster.

Yes. Turning the volume up makes the part of your device that pushes the speaker (the amplifier) work harder, like pressing a gas pedal makes the engine burn more fuel. Louder sound means the speaker has to move farther and faster, which takes more electrical power, so the battery drains faster at 8/10 than at 3/10.

How much faster depends on what’s doing the work. If you’re using the built‑in speaker or wired headphones, your device supplies the power for the sound, so volume has a noticeable effect—especially near the top of the range. If you’re using Bluetooth headphones, the headphones have their own battery and do most of the work; turning them up drains the headphones more than the phone. Also remember other parts often dominate battery use: the screen and network (streaming over cellular) can use more power than the music itself. For the longest play time, keep the volume moderate, turn the screen off, and, if possible, play downloaded music or use Wi‑Fi.

Yes. Melatonin is generally safe, but you can take “too much” for your body. Think of melatonin as a dimmer switch or a whisper that tells your brain, “It’s night now.” Turning the whisper into a shout doesn’t make you sleep better; it often backfires. Too much can cause next‑day grogginess, dizziness, headache, nausea, irritability, vivid dreams or nightmares, and sometimes changes in blood pressure or heart rate. It’s rarely life‑threatening in adults, but children are more vulnerable, and accidental ingestions (especially gummies) have led to emergency visits. Another wrinkle: timing matters as much as dose—taking it at the wrong time or in high amounts can shift your body clock and make sleep worse, like giving yourself jet lag.

Practical guide: the body naturally makes about 0.3 mg. Many adults do well with 0.5–1 mg taken 1–2 hours before bedtime; most don’t need more than 3 mg. For children, pregnancy, or long‑term use, talk to a clinician first. Choose reputable brands (quality can vary), keep out of children’s reach, and avoid driving or alcohol after taking it. If you took too much, skip the next dose, rest, and expect symptoms to fade within about a day. Seek urgent care or call poison control if there’s severe confusion, fainting, trouble breathing, persistent vomiting, seizures, or if a child took an unknown or large amount. Be cautious if you use blood thinners, blood pressure or diabetes medications, or sedatives, as melatonin can interact with them.
